strengths: The paper makes a useful diagnostic distinction between binding information encoded within each modality and its accessibility through CLIP’s cross-modal similarity. This is a meaningful refinement of claims that CLIP behaves like a bag-of-words model.

The main empirical results are substantial: frozen-encoder probes achieve 95–96% image accuracy and approximately 100% text accuracy on controlled datasets, while LABCLIP improves cross-modal binding from near chance to 94–97%. Appendix experiments extend the findings across three CLIP backbones.

The evaluation combines controlled synthetic datasets, conjunctive search, and real-world benchmarks. PUG:SPARE addresses an identified positional shortcut in PUG:SPAR, and the CC3M-trained adapter provides useful evidence beyond COCO-specific adaptation.

LABCLIP is simple and practically attractive: a small linear transformation improves compositional retrieval without updating encoders. The paper includes hard-negative ablations, downstream evaluations, and analyses of probe alignment.
weaknesses: The central conclusion is stronger than the evidence warrants. Recovering task-relevant signals with supervised probes and an adapter establishes that useful information exists, but does not establish that misalignment is the sole source of binding failures. Unimodal experiments primarily concern synthetic colors and shapes/animals; real-world cross-modal gains do not independently verify unimodal binding there.

The claimed BoW sanity check is not a valid binding-free control. Training an encoder to predict attribute counts does not enforce invariance to attribute-object permutations in its hidden embeddings. Its 66% image and 85% text probing accuracies therefore cannot establish what a true BoW representation can recover. Moreover, the 1/8 random baseline understates what knowing the two colors alone permits. An explicitly permutation-invariant representation and matched swapped-binding examples would provide stronger controls.

The generalization claims and split descriptions are inconsistent. Section 4.1 says individual attribute-object pairs are unique to each split, whereas Appendix A.5 clarifies that only complete two-object combinations are held out and individual bindings remain available during training. The reported 1.29% result under the Lewis et al. split demonstrates a substantial limitation on unseen-binding generalization. The main text should clearly distinguish recognition of familiar bindings in new scenes from learning transferable compositional structure.

The practical contribution is incompletely positioned against existing lightweight adaptation or metric-learning approaches. NegCLIP is useful as a full-fine-tuning reference, but comparisons with other frozen-feature adapters or constrained linear mappings would clarify whether LABCLIP contributes more than a straightforward supervised bilinear similarity. The reported efficiency advantage also lacks a sufficiently detailed timing protocol.

Some performance claims obscure meaningful tradeoffs. Table 11 shows ImageNet accuracy falling from 56% to 46% and CIFAR-100 from 65% to 57% after COCO training, which is more than a slight degradation. LABCLIP also trails NegCLIP on several compositional metrics, including SugarCrepe Add and ARO order tests, so the assertion that it matches NegCLIP needs qualification.

Reproducibility and statistical support need improvement: results lack variation across seeds or splits, conjunctive-search testing uses only 100 images per object-count setting, the repeated 90/10/10 split ratio is invalid, and the multi-object probe’s output/loss specification is unclear when an object category has several colors. The abstract’s promised code link is also missing.

strengths: The distinction between information encoded within each modality and information accessible through cross-modal similarity is useful. The paper provides concrete evidence that poor image–text matching need not imply absent binding information.
Frozen-encoder probes achieve strong synthetic binding accuracy across three CLIP backbones. PUG:SPARE removes the positional shortcut identified in PUG:SPAR, strengthening the controlled evaluation.

The linear adapter produces substantial gains without encoder updates: on CLEVR, binding accuracy rises from 0.58 to 0.95; on real-world benchmarks, improvements include SugarCrepe Swap from 0.62 to 0.74 and COCO Recall@1 from 0.30 to 0.41.

The appendix includes useful additional experiments: training without hard negatives, transforming image embeddings instead of text embeddings, spatial evaluation, and downstream transfer. Reusing cached embeddings is a practical benefit.
weaknesses: The central diagnosis is stronger than the evidence. Successful supervised probes and a learned bilinear similarity establish recoverable binding information on the evaluated distributions; they do not establish that misalignment is the sole cause of CLIP’s binding failures or that its encoders contain all necessary information. Direct unimodal evidence is restricted to synthetic settings, and image probing deteriorates with scene complexity.

The generalization protocol is described misleadingly in Section 4.1: it states that attribute–object binding pairs are unique to each split, whereas Appendix A.5 explicitly says individual pairs occur in training and only complete two-object combinations are held out. This distinction materially changes the interpretation. The reported 1.29% result on the stronger held-out-pair protocol further limits claims about compositional generalization.

The purported BoW control is not actually constrained to be a bag-of-words representation. Training a transformer to predict attribute counts does not prevent its hidden embeddings from retaining binding information. Its probe accuracies of 0.66 and 0.85 therefore cannot support the assertion that BoW representations lack binding structure. An explicitly permutation-invariant representation and an attribute-marginal baseline would provide cleaner controls.

The conjunctive-search experiment does not clearly establish that positive and negative images have matched color counts, shape counts, and total object counts. Adding or replacing a target can alter these marginal statistics. Without explicit balancing or a count-based control, this experiment does not independently rule out an explanation based on unbound features.

The methodological contribution is a standard linear transformation trained with an existing hard-negative strategy, so its significance rests primarily on the diagnosis. Comparisons with other lightweight alignment or adapter approaches are missing. Moreover, the claim that LABCLIP matches NegCLIP is too broad: Table 4 shows gaps on several benchmarks, while Table 11 reveals substantial downstream costs, including ImageNet accuracy falling from 0.56 to 0.46 and CIFAR-100 from 0.65 to 0.57.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting need improvement. The manuscript provides hyperparameter ranges rather than selected configurations, repeatedly states an impossible 90/10/10 split, and does not report variability across seeds or splits. The multi-object prediction procedure is under-specified despite allowing several colors per object category, and the promised code link is absent. Overall, the empirical signal is promising, but the controls and claim calibration leave the paper marginally below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper makes a useful diagnostic distinction between information encoded within each modality and information accessible through cross-modal similarity. This directly challenges the inference that poor image–text matching necessarily implies missing binding information.

The central finding has substantial quantitative support: frozen ViT-L/14 embeddings achieve 95–96% image-probe accuracy and approximately 100% text-probe accuracy on CLEVR and PUG:SPARE. Results across three CLIP backbones strengthen the evidence beyond a single model.

LABCLIP provides a simple, effective demonstration that encoder retraining is unnecessary for substantial improvements on the evaluated binding tasks. Synthetic matching accuracy rises from approximately chance to 94–97%, and real-world gains extend to CC3M-trained models evaluated on ARO and SugarCrepe.

PUG:SPARE addresses an identified positional shortcut in PUG:SPAR. The frozen-encoder design, standard-batch ablation, and downstream evaluations also add practical value and help characterize the intervention.
weaknesses: The conclusion that binding failures stem from misalignment rather than missing information is broader than the evidence establishes. The synthetic experiments primarily test new combinations of previously observed attribute–object pairs. Appendix A.5 reports only 1.29% performance under the harder Lewis et al. split that holds out individual pairs. This does not invalidate the narrower recoverability result, but substantially limits claims about compositional understanding. Section 4.1 also misleadingly describes individual binding pairs as exclusive to a split, contradicting the appendix.

The BoW sanity check is not a valid binding-free control: training an encoder to predict attribute counts does not enforce an order-invariant or binding-free representation. Its 66% image and 85% text probing accuracies therefore cannot establish the claimed absence of binding structure. An explicitly invariant representation and a matched pretrained attribute-only baseline would provide stronger controls.

The conjunctive-search experiment does not clearly establish that target-present and target-absent images have matched object counts and marginal feature statistics. Because the target is described as an added object, count or feature-frequency cues remain possible explanations unless explicitly controlled.

The algorithmic contribution is modest: a learned bilinear similarity with established hard-negative training. Comparisons against alternative frozen-feature adapters or metric-learning baselines would better establish its distinctiveness. The statement that LABCLIP matches NegCLIP is also too broad: Table 4 shows meaningful deficits on Flickr-PRC, COCO-PRC, and SugarCrepe Add.

Practical tradeoffs and reproducibility need clearer treatment. COCO-trained LABCLIP reduces ImageNet zero-shot accuracy from 56% to 46%, which is more than a slight degradation. Results lack uncertainty estimates, the reported 90/10/10 split is inconsistent with the numerical example, and the promised code link is absent. These issues prevent a stronger acceptance recommendation.
